title: Isabella and Ferdinand Marry in Secret
text:
In 1468 Isabella, half-sister of King Henry IV of Castile, was recognized as heir to the throne. Henry wanted her to marry the king of Portugal or a French prince, matches that would serve his own policy. Isabella, eighteen, chose for herself: her cousin Ferdinand, heir to the crown of Aragon.

Henry opposed the match, and Ferdinand had to cross hostile territory to reach her. According to the chroniclers, he traveled in disguise in October 1469 with a few companions, posing as a servant of merchants, and waited on the others at the inns. The couple met for the first time at Valladolid and were married there on 19 October 1469, with a papal dispensation for their kinship that was of doubtful validity.

When Henry died in 1474, Isabella proclaimed herself queen of Castile. Ferdinand's supporters argued that he, as a man, should rule. The question was settled in 1475 by an agreement at Segovia that defined their shared authority. They issued laws, coins and documents in both names. Later generations summed up the arrangement with a popular saying built on Ferdinand's personal motto, Tanto monta: each counted as much as the other.

Ruling together, the Catholic Monarchs united the crowns of Castile and Aragon, completed the conquest of Granada in 1492 and sponsored Columbus. Their reign also brought the Inquisition and the expulsion of the Jews, part of their joint legacy.
lesson: A marriage of equals works when power is shared openly and its terms are agreed. Partners who choose each other freely can achieve more together.
people: Isabella I of Castile, Ferdinand II of Aragon, Henry IV of Castile
source: Fernando del Pulgar, Cronica de los Reyes Catolicos; Concord of Segovia (1475); Peggy K. Liss, Isabel the Queen (1992)
